intro: Seattle logged nearly all of itself, and kept only pockets of what stood before. Seward Park holds a Douglas fir of 400 to 500 years with an eagle nest in it; a second old-growth survivor, Sylvia, stands in Kirkland after a 1993 storm took her crown. The rest are garden plantings: a giant sequoia on Capitol Hill, a Kubota Garden grand fir with two more of the garden's pines beside it, a state champion in the arboretum, and a poplar dated to the 1909 world's fair.
meta_description: Seattle's oldest trees: two old-growth Douglas firs, a Capitol Hill sequoia, three Kubota Garden conifers, a state champion and an 1909 poplar.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Seattle is the Big Tree in Seward Park, a Douglas fir of roughly 400 to 500 years standing in the old-growth remnant on the peninsula, with a bald eagle nest near its top. Nobody publishes exactly where it is in the park's 120 acres, so finding it is part of the walk, and the much younger fir the park's own leaflet starts you at is not it. A second old-growth survivor, Sylvia, stands in Kirkland's O.O. Denny Park at roughly 500 to 600 years, close enough in age that either tree could be the true elder; neither has been cored.
question_meta: The Big Tree in Seward Park, a Douglas fir of 400 to 500 years in Seattle's last old-growth remnant, is the city's oldest known tree.
question_context: Seattle has no register of individual trees, which shapes everything on this page. The city runs a Heritage Tree programme with the group PlantAmnesty and it names trees without publishing a dataset, the parks department's own file is a full street inventory rather than a selection, and Washington's state champion list records size rather than age. So every pin here is approximate, meaning we know the park and not the trunk, and two of the eight trees have no recorded age at all. That includes the giant sequoia on Capitol Hill, where the city's own tree-walk leaflet quotes a height and a diameter that belong to what the species can reach rather than to this tree, which is the kind of number that gets repeated until somebody checks it. We would rather say we do not know. Sylvia, the old-growth survivor in Kirkland, comes closest to challenging the Seward Park fir for the oldest-tree title, and neither has been cored to settle it. If you have a tape measure and ten minutes in Volunteer Park, you can settle the sequoia, and we will put your figure on the page.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Seattle?
faq.a: The Big Tree in Seward Park, a Douglas fir of roughly 400 to 500 years, standing in the old-growth remnant the city never logged. Sylvia, a similarly aged fir in Kirkland's O.O. Denny Park, may in fact be a little older; neither tree has been cored, so both stay honest estimates.

faq.q: How do I find the Big Tree?
faq.a: With some hunting. Its exact position in the park's 120 acres is not published, and the large fir the park's own leaflet starts you at is a much younger tree. Follow the interior trails rather than the shoreline loop.

faq.q: Are Seattle's old trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Every tree on this page stands in a public park, arboretum or garden, and every one is free to see. The Washington Park Arboretum charges nothing to walk through either.

faq.q: What trees stand in Kubota Garden?
faq.a: Three: a grand fir the loggers left standing before Fujitaro Kubota built his garden around it, and two of the specimen conifers he planted afterwards, a Tanyosho pine and a Japanese white pine, both identified on the garden's own tree walk.

faq.q: Is Sylvia the oldest tree in Seattle?
faq.a: Possibly. She is a Douglas fir of roughly 500 to 600 years in Kirkland, close in age to the Seward Park fir usually named the city's oldest. Neither tree has been cored, so we cannot settle it and list Seward Park's fir as the answer by convention rather than certainty.

trees.name: Seward Park's Big Tree

location.address: Seward Park old-growth forest interior, 5895 Lake Washington Blvd S, Seattle, WA 98118 (exact grove location within the ~120-acre old-growth remnant is not published by any source found)

trees.access: Free, city park, open trails during park hours
trees.transport: King County Metro Route 50 stops at Seward Park Ave S and S Orcas St, at the park entrance; the old-growth interior is a further walk into the peninsula
trees.story:
Seattle's oldest known tree still carries the burn marks of two fires, one in 1508 and one in 1701, when the Puget lowlands went up and this Douglas fir did not. The scarred bark is on the trunk, which is about seven feet across. The tree is around 150 feet tall.

How old is a matter of who you ask. Friends of Seward Park, the group that looks after the forest, says 500 years. Seattle Magazine says over 400. Somewhere in that band is the honest answer, and either end of it means this tree was a mature fir before any European saw Puget Sound. Bald eagles have nested in it.

It used to carry a Heritage Tree plaque. The plaque was taken down because the number of people walking in to see it was wearing the ground away over the roots, which tells you both how good the tree is and how to behave around it.

No source publishes where it stands inside the 120 acres of old growth on the Bailey Peninsula, so the pin marks the park rather than the trunk and finding it is part of the afternoon. One warning: the young fir the park's printed tree walk starts with, near the Audubon building, is a different tree and a couple of centuries younger.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the burn scars on the trunk, left by fires in 1508 and 1701, and by the size of it, about seven feet through and 150 feet tall. It stands deep in the old growth, not the young fir near the Audubon building.

trees.name: The Volunteer Park Giant Sequoia

location.address: Near E Highland Drive, Volunteer Park, 1247 15th Ave E, Seattle, WA 98112

trees.access: Free, city park, open daylight hours
trees.transport: Metro routes 10 and 12 stop within a few blocks on 15th Ave E / E Galer St; about a 5 minute walk
trees.story:
The only measurements ever published about this sequoia are not measurements of this sequoia. The city's own tree walk, which lists it as stop 9 on the north east loop of Volunteer Park, describes it growing to 280 feet with a trunk 26 feet through. Those are the figures for the species, the largest tree on earth by volume, and nobody has put a tape around this particular trunk.

What the leaflet does confirm is the tree: a good giant sequoia standing near East Highland Drive, with the thick spongy bark that is the easiest way to identify one, and the only way to identify one without looking up.

Its age is unrecorded. Volunteer Park was landscaped by the Olmsted Brothers between 1904 and 1912, and it is tempting to date the sequoia from that work, but no source connects this tree to it, so it stays undated here rather than dated by association.

Which means there is a question on this page that somebody in Capitol Hill can answer. If you have a planting record, a nursery receipt, an old photograph of this corner of the park or simply a tape measure and a free afternoon, tell us and we will fill the gap in.

The pin marks the north east corner of the park rather than the tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thick spongy bark, which is how you tell a giant sequoia without looking up. It stands near East Highland Drive, stop 9 on the city tree walk's north east loop of Volunteer Park.

trees.name: The Grand Fir of Kubota Garden

location.address: Base of the Spring Pond, below the Terrace Overlook, Kubota Garden, 9817 55th Ave S, Seattle, WA 98178

trees.access: Free, city park (Seattle Parks), open daylight hours
trees.transport: Metro Route 106 stops on Renton Ave S near the garden entrance; about a 5-10 minute walk
trees.story:
When Fujitaro Kubota bought this land in 1927 it had been logged, and this grand fir was one of the few trees the loggers had left. Everything else you walk past in Kubota Garden was planted afterwards, around it. The garden is the newcomer.

It now stands 139 feet tall at the base of the Spring Pond, below the Terrace Overlook, and the tree walk that covers the garden estimates it at 200 years old. That figure comes from a single document, the walk produced jointly by the city's Trees for Seattle programme and the Kubota Garden Foundation, and no second source has confirmed it, so read it as a good estimate rather than a settled number. Grand firs live comfortably beyond 250 years, so the estimate sits well within what the species does.

The interest here is the contrast. Kubota spent decades building a Japanese garden out of Pacific Northwest plants, and this fir is the piece of the actual Pacific Northwest forest that was already on the site when he started, a survivor of the original woodland standing over ponds and stone that were arranged much later.

The garden is free and open in daylight hours. The pin marks the entrance rather than the tree, so walk in and head for the Spring Pond below the Terrace Overlook.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one tree here nobody planted: 139 feet of grand fir the loggers left, with the whole garden arranged around it afterwards. It stands at the base of the Spring Pond, below the Terrace Overlook.

trees.name: The Bigcone Douglas Fir of Washington Park Arboretum

location.address: Upper Trail, just south of the Pacific Connections New Zealand Forest Garden, Washington Park Arboretum, 2300 Arboretum Drive E, Seattle, WA 98112

trees.access: Free, public arboretum, open daylight hours
trees.transport: Metro Route 11 stops on Madison St near the Arboretum entrances; several trailheads within a 5-10 minute walk of stops
trees.story:
This fir is about a thousand miles from where its species grows wild. Pseudotsuga macrocarpa is native only to the mountains of southern California, and the largest one known in Washington State is standing in a public arboretum in Seattle.

It was recorded as a state champion in Robert Van Pelt's 2003 survey of Washington's biggest trees, and the University of Washington Botanic Gardens, who run the Arboretum, list it as one of their champions and have been re-measuring it. Both of those threads run back to the same 2003 survey, so the title rests on one original piece of fieldwork rather than two.

The reason to walk out and see it is in the name. Bigcone Douglas fir carries by far the largest cones in its genus, several times the size of the ones that litter every pavement in this part of the world, and a tree that size drops them where you can pick one up. It is a curiosity rather than a giant, and it is the sort of thing an arboretum exists for.

No age or girth has been published for it. It stands on the Upper Trail just south of the Pacific Connections New Zealand Forest Garden, at the south end of the Arboretum; the pin marks the Arboretum itself.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the cones, by far the largest in its genus and several times the size of the ones on every pavement here. It stands on the Upper Trail just south of the Pacific Connections New Zealand Forest Garden.

trees.name: The AYPE Lombardy Poplar

location.address: Corner of Stevens Way and Grant Lane, across from Architecture Hall, University of Washington campus, Seattle, WA 98195

trees.transport: Link light rail U District or UW Station; multiple Metro routes serve the campus; short walk to Stevens Way
trees.story:
This poplar is a leftover from a world's fair. The Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition of 1909 was held on this part of the University of Washington campus, and the university's own campus tree tour dates this burly trunk to that event, which makes it about 115 to 120 years old and one of the few living things on the grounds that saw the fair.

The building across the street backs the date up. Architecture Hall was built as the Fine Arts Palace for the same exposition, and it and the poplar have stood facing each other on the corner of Stevens Way ever since, one of them looking rather more temporary than the other.

A Lombardy poplar is a narrow upright form of black poplar, grown from cuttings rather than seed, which is why they all look identical and why they turn up in rows along drives and boundaries. This one is not a record holder and does not claim to be: bigger Lombardy poplars have been claimed elsewhere in Seattle. Its distinction is that somebody wrote down where it came from.

Campus grounds are open and free. The pin uses the campus centre, so navigate to the corner of Stevens Way and Grant Lane, opposite Architecture Hall, and look up.

best_time.label: late October into November, when it turns yellow

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the narrow upright shape of a Lombardy poplar and the burly trunk underneath it. It stands on the corner of Stevens Way and Grant Lane, facing Architecture Hall, the fair's old Fine Arts Palace.

trees.name: Sylvia

location.address: O.O. Denny Park, 12032 Holmes Point Drive NE, Kirkland, WA 98034 (in the old-growth grove along the creek; the park does not publish a pin for the tree itself)

trees.access: Free, public park, open daylight hours
trees.transport: About 13 km from central Seattle across Lake Washington; no direct bus, so it is a drive or a ride to Holmes Point Drive NE and a short walk into the grove
trees.story:
Sylvia was the biggest tree in King County until the morning of 20 January 1993, when an inauguration day windstorm came up Lake Washington and took her top off. She was 255 feet then. She is a good deal shorter now and still standing, which is the part worth walking for: a Douglas fir about eight metres round, growing here since roughly the time Constantinople fell.

The snapped crown is not damage so much as biography. A Douglas fir that loses its leader does not die, it reorganises, pushing side branches upward into a candelabra of new tops. Sylvia has been doing that for thirty years and the result looks nothing like the clean spire in a forestry photograph.

She stands in what is left of the lowland old growth that once ran unbroken from the lake to the Cascades. O.O. Denny Park keeps about forty acres of it, given to Seattle by the Denny family and now looked after by Kirkland. The trail in from Holmes Point Drive follows a creek under trees that were already large when the first mill opened on the far shore.

We cannot give you a pin on the trunk. Follow the creek trail and look for the one with no proper top.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the missing top, snapped off in the 1993 windstorm and since replaced by side branches growing up into a candelabra, on a trunk about eight metres round. It stands along the creek trail.
trees.verify_notes: 2026-09-10: a photo pass flagged this as possibly dead, because a ground plaque in one candidate reads 'Toppled January 20, 1993'. Checked: the tree stands. That storm took her TOP off, not the tree, which is what our story says and what all three sources say. The Seattle Times piece is titled 'Meet Sylvia, the topless fir in Kirkland's O.O. Denny Park' and describes walking to her; a Douglas fir that loses its leader reorganises into a candelabra of new tops rather than dying. The plaque's wording is loose. Do not reopen this on the strength of that plaque again.

trees.name: The Tanyosho Pine of Kubota Garden

location.address: Historic Core Garden, near the Heart Bridge, Kubota Garden, 9817 55th Ave S, Seattle, WA 98118

trees.access: Free; Kubota Garden is a public city park, open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Rainier Beach neighbourhood, south Seattle; nearest Metro bus stops on Renton Ave S, roughly 10 minute walk
trees.story:
Fujitaro Kubota planted somewhere between fifteen and twenty of these pines along the drive of his garden. This is the only one left.

The early aerial photographs show what he made: a row of tanyosho pines, the umbrella-shaped form of the Japanese red pine, lining the drive closely enough to filter the light into a kind of tunnel. Kubota was a Japanese immigrant gardener who founded the garden in 1927, in what is now Rainier Beach. It became a City Historical Landmark in 1981 and a public park in 1987.

The pines did not all make it. The city's own tree walk puts it plainly: after many winter storms and a changing climate, only one of the original trees, about ninety years old when that guide was written, is still standing. A handful of replacements have gone in over the past twenty years, so the drive is slowly becoming a row again, with one old tree among the young ones.

That old one is the tree worth finding. It stands in the Historic Core Garden near the Heart Bridge, stop eight on the city's Kubota Garden tree walk. Entry is free and the garden is open daily. The pin marks the garden rather than the pine, so bring the tree walk and look for the Heart Bridge.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one old umbrella-shaped pine among a handful of young replacements planted in the last twenty years. It stands in the Historic Core Garden near the Heart Bridge, stop eight on the city tree walk.

trees.name: The Japanese White Pine of Kubota Garden

location.address: Japanese Garden section, Kubota Garden, 9817 55th Ave S, Seattle, WA 98118

trees.access: Free; Kubota Garden is a public city park, open daily, no entry fee
trees.transport: Rainier Beach neighbourhood, south Seattle; nearest Metro bus stops on Renton Ave S, roughly 10 minute walk
trees.story:
Of every tree in the garden he spent his life making, this was Fujitaro Kubota's favourite. The city's own tree walk says so, and it is the kind of detail that changes how you look at a tree.

It is a Japanese white pine, and what caught his eye is still there to see: a white line running along each needle, which, in the guide's words, exudes brightness and light. It has been pruned carefully for more than eighty years, and what the guide praises is not its size but its limbs and lines, which is what that much patient cutting produces.

That pruning is its real age record. Nobody has published a planting date, only that the shaping has gone on for over eight decades, and it cannot be older than the garden itself, which Kubota, a Japanese immigrant gardener, founded here in 1927. So somewhere between eighty and a hundred years is the honest range. If you know when it went in, tell us.

The garden around it became a city landmark in 1981 and a free public park in 1987, and the pine has been tended through all of it. It stands in the Japanese Garden section, stop fourteen on the city's Kubota Garden tree walk. The pin marks the garden rather than the tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the white line along each needle, which gives it its bright look, and by limbs shaped by eighty years of careful pruning. It stands in the Japanese Garden section, stop fourteen on the city tree walk.
